q: Where does Helm (v3 and v4) store the state of a release such as its revisions and values?
options: In annotations on every resource it created
In a Tiller pod in `kube-system`
In `~/.helm` on the machine that ran `helm install`
In Secrets of type `helm.sh/release.v1` in the release's namespace
explain: Helm has had no server component since v3. Each revision is stored as a Secret named `sh.helm.release.v1.<release>.v<revision>` in the release namespace, which is how `helm history`, `get values` and `rollback` work from any machine with access.

q: Your pipeline runs `helm upgrade --install shipit ./chart --set image.tag=$SHA`. A bad image makes the rollout hang and the pipeline times out, leaving the Deployment half-rolled. Which flags fix this behaviour?
options: `--reuse-values`
`--dry-run=server`
`--wait --timeout 5m --rollback-on-failure` (`--atomic` in Helm 3)
`--force-replace`
explain: `--wait` makes Helm block until resources are ready, `--timeout` bounds it, and `--rollback-on-failure`/`--atomic` rolls back to the previous revision on failure. `--force-replace` deletes and recreates resources; `--reuse-values` is about values; a dry run deploys nothing.

q: Values are given as: chart `values.yaml` sets `replicaCount: 1`, `-f base.yaml` sets 2, `-f prod.yaml` sets 4, and `--set replicaCount=3`. What value is used?
explain: Precedence is chart defaults < `-f` files in order (later wins) < `--set`. So `--set replicaCount=3` overrides everything.

q: After bumping `appVersion`, `helm upgrade` fails with `spec.selector: Invalid value: ... field is immutable`. What is the root cause?
options: The Deployment's selector labels include a value that changes between releases, such as the app version
The Service selector does not match the pods
Helm 4 does not support upgrades of Deployments created by Helm 3
The chart version was not bumped
explain: `spec.selector` of a Deployment cannot change after creation. Selector labels must be stable (name + instance). Versions belong in the general labels only. Fixing it requires replacing the Deployment once.

q: You change a value that only affects a ConfigMap in your chart. After `helm upgrade`, the pods still use the old configuration. What is the idiomatic chart fix?
options: Use a pre-upgrade hook that deletes all pods
Add a `checksum/config` annotation to the pod template computed from the rendered ConfigMap
Mount the ConfigMap with `subPath`
Set `imagePullPolicy: Always`
explain: Environment variables from a ConfigMap are read at container start. An annotation like `checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}` changes the pod template whenever the ConfigMap changes, triggering a normal rolling update.

q: Which statements about Kustomize are true? (select all)
options: The `images` field can change an image's name, tag or digest without writing a patch
Kustomize is built into kubectl (`kubectl apply -k`, `kubectl kustomize`)
Bases must be written as Go templates
Kustomize stores release revisions so you can roll back with `kubectl rollback -k`
`configMapGenerator` appends a content hash to the name and updates references, so config changes roll Deployments
explain: Kustomize transforms plain YAML (no templates), is embedded in kubectl, and has generators with hash suffixes and an images transformer. It has no release concept or rollback; you roll back by applying an earlier Git revision.

q: Your team runs three of its own Node.js services across dev/staging/prod, and installs Argo CD and kube-prometheus-stack. Which approach is most conventional?
options: Only use plain `kubectl apply` with sed replacements
Write Helm charts for Argo CD and Prometheus yourself; copy YAML per environment for your services
Fork every third-party chart into your repo and edit the templates
Install third-party components from their upstream Helm charts; manage your own services with Kustomize overlays (or one simple chart per service)
explain: Upstream charts are the supported way to install third-party software, with values for configuration. For your own apps, Kustomize overlays or a small chart with per-environment values files both work well. Copy-paste and sed scripts drift; forking charts makes upgrades painful.

q: Which are among the four OpenGitOps principles? (select all)
options: Deployments are triggered by CI pushing to the cluster
Continuously reconciled
Versioned and immutable storage of desired state
Declarative desired state
Pulled automatically by software agents
explain: The principles are declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled. CI pushing with cluster credentials is the push model GitOps replaces.

q: An Argo CD Application shows `Synced` but `Degraded`. What does that tell you?
options: Self-heal is disabled
The live objects match Git, but at least one resource is unhealthy (for example a Deployment whose pods are failing)
Argo CD cannot reach the Git repository
Git and the cluster differ
explain: Sync status compares desired (Git) and live state; health status evaluates whether resources work. You can apply exactly what is in Git and still have crashing pods; then debug the workload, not Argo CD.

q: With Argo CD self-heal enabled, a Deployment managed by an HPA keeps flapping between 2 replicas and the HPA's desired count. Why, and what is the fix?
options: Pruning deletes the HPA on each sync
The HPA is broken; delete it
The manifest in Git sets `replicas: 2`, so Argo CD reverts the HPA's change; omit `replicas` when autoscaling (or ignore that field with `ignoreDifferences`)
Argo CD does not support HPAs
explain: Two controllers fight over `spec.replicas`. Let the HPA own the field: do not set it in the manifest (charts usually wrap `replicas` in `if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled`), or tell Argo CD to ignore the difference.

q: Someone runs `kubectl edit` on a production Deployment managed by Argo CD with automated sync, `prune: true` and `selfHeal: true`. What happens?
options: Argo CD detects the drift and reverts the live object to match Git
The change persists until the next Git commit
Argo CD commits the change back to Git
Argo CD deletes the Deployment because it was modified
explain: Self-heal means drift in the cluster triggers a sync back to the Git state. Prune is about deleting resources removed from Git. Argo CD never writes manual cluster changes back to Git.

q: How should you handle a database password in a GitOps repository?
options: Store it in `values.yaml` in a private repository
Pass it with `--set` in the Argo CD Application
Commit a Kubernetes Secret; base64 is encoding enough
Commit an ExternalSecret (or a SealedSecret / SOPS-encrypted file) and let an in-cluster controller produce the Secret
explain: Base64 is not encryption, and private repos still leak through clones, forks and CI logs. External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets and SOPS keep only references or ciphertext in Git.

q: `helm template` renders fine, but `helm install` fails because a template uses `lookup` to read an existing Secret. Why did rendering succeed?
options: `helm template` ignores all functions
`lookup` is disabled in Helm 4
`helm template` does not contact the cluster, so `lookup` returns an empty result instead of failing
`lookup` only works with `--set`
explain: Client-side rendering has no cluster access; `lookup` returns an empty map. Charts relying on `lookup` behave differently between `template`/GitOps rendering and a real install, which is a reason to avoid it in charts meant for Argo CD.
